```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, message = FALSE)
has_gg <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
```

How good is a forecast? The future is unknown, but the past can be used
as a test: fit a model to the years up to some year in the past (the
*origin*), forecast the following years, and compare the forecast with
what was observed. Repeating this from several origins gives a
*rolling-origin backtest* (Tashman 2000). This vignette explains the
design and the scores, and compares three models on one data set.

## Data and models

Deaths and populations in England by sex and deprivation quintile,
2001-2019 (ONS). Three models, chosen as examples:

* a **random walk with drift** per age (`rwd()`): each log rate continues
  its average change of the past. It is a standard benchmark in
  forecasting: a model that does not beat it adds little;
* **Lee-Carter** (`lee_carter()`), one model per stratum;
* **Li-Lee** (`li_lee(common_by = "sex")`), quintiles of each sex pooled
  around a common trend.

```{r}
library(mortensor)
library(data.table)
x <- mt_data(deaths = ons_data, population = ons_data, by = c("sex", "imd_decile"), age = "age_group",
             value = c(deaths = "all_causes", population = "population"))
x <- mt_as_exposure(x, type = "midyear")
x <- mt_group_levels(x, "imd_decile", function(d) paste0("Q", ceiling(as.numeric(d) / 2)), name = "quintile")
models <- list("random walk" = rwd(), "Lee-Carter" = lee_carter(), "Li-Lee" = li_lee(common_by = "sex"))
```

## The design

Seven origins, 2008 to 2014, each forecasting five years:

```{r, eval = has_gg, fig.height = 3}
mt_plot_backtest_design(x, origins = 2008:2014, h = 5)
```

Every model, and every preprocessing step such as smoothing, is fitted
anew at each origin from the training years only, so no information from
the test years leaks into the forecast. Each test year is forecast
several times from different origins and horizons, which averages over
the particular events of a single period.

```{r}
bt <- mt_compare(models, x, origins = 2008:2014, h = 5, n_draws = 200, quantities = "life_expectancy")
```

The forecasts are *predictive*: they describe the observed death rates
of the test years, including the Poisson noise of the counts, because the
observed rates are what they are compared with.

## Scores

### Interval coverage

A 95% interval should contain the observed value in about 95% of the
cases. The *empirical coverage* is the share of observed values inside
the interval: below the nominal level, the intervals are too narrow;
above it, too wide.

```{r, eval = has_gg, fig.height = 3.5}
mt_plot_coverage(bt)
```

Coverage alone can be gamed: a very wide interval always covers. It is
read together with a score that also rewards narrow intervals.

### CRPS

The continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) compares the whole
forecast distribution with the observed value: it is the integral of the
squared difference between the forecast's cumulative distribution and a
step at the observed value (Gneiting and Raftery 2007). The figure shades
the difference between the two curves; squared and summed over the axis, it
gives the CRPS:

```{r, echo = FALSE, eval = has_gg, fig.height = 3}
z <- seq(-0.6, 0.6, by = 0.002)
fcs <- data.table(forecast = rep(c("sharp, but off target", "wide, centred"), each = length(z)), z = z,
                  cdf = c(pnorm(z, 0.15, 0.05), pnorm(z, 0, 0.2)))
fcs[, observed := as.numeric(z >= 0)]
crps_norm <- function(m, s) s * ((0 - m) / s * (2 * pnorm((0 - m) / s) - 1) + 2 * dnorm((0 - m) / s) - 1 / sqrt(pi))
lab <- data.table(forecast = c("sharp, but off target", "wide, centred"),
                  text = sprintf("CRPS = %.3f", c(crps_norm(0.15, 0.05), crps_norm(0, 0.2))))
ggplot2::ggplot(fcs, ggplot2::aes(z)) +
  ggplot2::geom_ribbon(ggplot2::aes(ymin = pmin(cdf, observed), ymax = pmax(cdf, observed)), fill = "#D95F02",
                       alpha = 0.3) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(ggplot2::aes(y = cdf), colour = "#1B9E77", linewidth = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::geom_step(ggplot2::aes(y = observed), colour = "grey30") +
  ggplot2::geom_text(data = lab, ggplot2::aes(x = -0.55, y = 0.9, label = text), hjust = 0, size = 3.5) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(ggplot2::vars(forecast)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Forecast error of the log death rate", y = "Cumulative probability",
                subtitle = "Green: forecast distribution; grey: observed value (0); shaded: their difference") +
  theme_mortensor()
```

A forecast that puts its probability close to the observed value has a
small area. The CRPS punishes both a distribution that is off target and
one that is wider than necessary. For a forecast without uncertainty it
equals the absolute error, so it is in the unit of the forecast quantity:
for log death rates, a CRPS of 0.05 means errors of roughly 5% of the
rate; for life expectancy it is in years. Lower is better.

The *weighted interval score* (WIS, Bracher et al. 2021) approximates the
CRPS from a few central intervals; it is reported as well and ranks
models in the same way.

### Point errors

`mae` and `rmse` are the mean absolute and the root mean squared error of
the forecast median: they ignore the intervals. `mase` divides the
absolute error by the mean absolute year-to-year change of the training data
(Hyndman and Koehler 2006): below 1, the forecast errs less than the
typical change of a single year.

### PIT

The probability integral transform (PIT) is the share of forecast draws
below the observed value. For calibrated forecasts it is spread evenly
between 0 and 1, so its histogram is flat. A U shape means that the
observed values often fall in the tails, outside intervals that are too
narrow; a slope means that the forecasts are systematically too high or
too low (Gneiting, Balabdaoui and Raftery 2007).

```{r, eval = has_gg, fig.height = 3}
mt_plot_pit(bt)
```

All three histograms rise to the right: the observed rates were more
often above the forecast median than below it. The forecasts were too
optimistic, because the decline of mortality in England slowed after
2011. Lee-Carter and Li-Lee also pile up at both ends (a U shape): their
intervals are too narrow.

## Comparing the models

```{r}
mt_score_table(bt, metrics = c("crps", "rmse", "cov80", "cov95"))
```

The columns without suffix score the log death rates of all cells; the
columns with `_le` score life expectancy at birth (in years), computed
from the same forecasts. Rates and life expectancy can rank models
differently, because life expectancy depends on how the errors of the
ages add up: for the rates Li-Lee is the most accurate (CRPS 0.067) and
the random walk the least (0.085), for life expectancy the random walk and
Lee-Carter are equal (0.29 years) and Li-Lee is the least accurate (0.34
years). Choose the target that the analysis is about.

```{r, eval = has_gg, fig.height = 3.5}
mt_plot_scores(bt)
```

All three models get worse with the horizon, as they should. The
random walk has wide intervals: its 95% coverage is close to nominal
(0.92), and its 50% and 80% intervals cover about as often as they
should. The 95% intervals of Lee-Carter and Li-Lee cover 0.79 and 0.81
of the observed rates, fewer at longer horizons: they describe the
uncertainty of a fixed trend and the Poisson noise of the deaths, while
the trend of English mortality changed after 2011. "Tuning and
recalibration" shows how to widen intervals to the errors of recent
forecasts, and "Choosing and combining models" how mixtures of models do.

## Is the difference larger than chance?

Mean scores over seven origins depend on the particular years. The
Diebold-Mariano test (Diebold and Mariano 1995) asks whether two models
differ in accuracy by more than the origins vary. `mt_dm_test()` computes
it for each horizon from the mean score of each origin, so the many cells
of one forecast count once. Forecasts from neighbouring origins overlap
in their test years, so the differences between origins are
autocorrelated. By default the test estimates their variance with the
equal-weighted cosine (EWC) estimator and takes critical values from a t
distribution with few degrees of freedom (Lazarus et al. 2018; Coroneo
and Iacone 2020). The older version, with the autocovariances up to lag
`h - 1` and the small-sample correction of Harvey, Leybourne and Newbold
(1997), rejects a true null hypothesis too often with few overlapping
origins: in simulations with seven origins, in 10% to 27% of the samples
at the nominal 5% level (see `?mt_dm_test`; `varestimator = "acf"` gives
that version).

```{r}
dm <- mt_dm_test(bt, ref = "Li-Lee")
dm[target == "rate", list(model, horizon, mean_diff, statistic, df, p_value)]
```

A positive `mean_diff` means a higher CRPS than Li-Lee, so a less
accurate forecast. Li-Lee forecast the rates more accurately than the
random walk at every horizon, with p-values from 0.007 to 0.14 (0.07 over
all horizons). Li-Lee and Lee-Carter differ little, with p-values from
0.57 to 0.94: this backtest cannot tell them apart.

```{r}
dm[target == "life_expectancy", list(model, horizon, mean_diff, statistic, p_value)]
```

For life expectancy, the random walk and Lee-Carter were more accurate
than Li-Lee at every horizon, but no difference is significant (p-values
from 0.19 to 0.54). With seven origins the test has one degree of freedom
(`df`) and detects only large and consistent differences. The row `"all"`
averages over the horizons.

## How far to trust a backtest

* Seven origins of one country are few, and the test years overlap; a
  difference of a few percent in the CRPS can be noise, as
  `mt_dm_test()` shows.
* A backtest scores the past. If the future differs from the test period
  (a pandemic, a policy change), so will the accuracy.
* Compare models on the same origins, horizons and cells, as
  `mt_compare()` does. Suppressed cells that were estimated are not
  scored.
